entry.title: Unredacted 1964 FBI Letter to Martin Luther King Jr. Examined by Historians
entry.content:
Links: vox.com | source | hacker news

In 1964, top FBI officials sent an anonymous, threatening letter and surveillance recordings of extramarital affairs to civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. in an effort to compel him to commit suicide. Directed by William Sullivan under FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover, the blackmail campaign followed years of intense government monitoring designed to discredit King's leadership and activism.

Yale historian Beverly Gage later unearthed a fully unredacted version of the document from archival records, revealing details previously concealed by government redactions. The text explicitly derided King's honors, including his Nobel Peace Prize, and warned him that he had 34 days to take his own life, highlighting the severe abuses of domestic intelligence agencies during the civil rights era.

entry.title: SimCity's Performance Optimization Techniques for 16 MHz Hardware Examined
entry.content:
Links: larstofus.com | discussion | hacker news

The article examines how early development teams successfully ran complex simulation games like the original 1989 SimCity on constrained 16 MHz hardware. By analyzing the open-source Micropolis codebase, the piece highlights how core simulation systems—such as traffic, fire, and crime—were updated across multiple frames rather than all at once every frame.

This technique of distributing computational workloads across frames avoids performance bottlenecks without noticeably degrading gameplay responsiveness. The author notes that similar frame-budgeting principles extend to modern graphics and rendering pipelines, such as reflection cubemaps in Assetto Corsa and dynamic lighting in Unreal Engine.
